chapter_theme: Under the heading அறம் செய்தல், fifteen verses on doing aram: the rich give easily, aram rather than the hoard is the reserve for need, it serves both worlds, it must be done before illness and death and while the rare human birth lasts, begun aram must not be dropped, a few days of the best will do, guarded wealth is lost anyway, grace is its root, and aram or penance practised falsely binds the deceiver.

357.reading: For those whose wealth lets them live enjoying the best, doing aram and becoming gracious is, the verse tells the lord of the hills where bamboo clashes with bamboo, only like setting something more on top of a load already carried.
357.nuance: The proverb is read for its ease: the rich already bear wealth, and adding giving to it costs them little. It could also be read as an added weight that the rich should take on gladly; the image does not settle which.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is the way of putting more on top along with the load

story.act: no story; the proverb's porter takes a little more on a load already borne

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram and grace come easily to those who already have wealth

358.reading: The verse says not to take stored wealth for a reserve, but to enjoy it, give it out on both sides and do aram looking to the fit occasion, and calls that the true reserve for the time of need.
358.nuance: The proverb's phrase எய்ப்பினில் வைப்பு, the store kept for the time of exhaustion, is taken from the hoard and given to aram. இருபாலும் 'on both sides' may be oneself and others, or this world and the next.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is called the store for the time of exhaustion

story.act: no story; the proverb's saving for hard times is redefined

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram done at the fit place, not the hoard, is the reserve for need

359.reading: When the worthy come by abundant great wealth, the verse tells a slender-waisted woman, they make it a protection even for where they go after death, like one who chews the green cane and also boils it into jaggery.
359.nuance: The proverb is read as using the cane both ways, tasting some now and turning the rest into a sweet that keeps, so wealth serves both the present and the hereafter. It might instead set chewing against boiling as waste against keeping.

pazhamozhi.literal: chewing the green sugarcane and making jaggery of it

story.act: no story; the proverb's cane is both eaten and turned into a sweet that lasts

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy use great wealth so that it also protects them in the world to come

360.reading: Aram wins fame for one still in this world and is sweetness for one who has passed to the other, so for one who does good aram every day, both worlds are like a forked road whose two branches both go well.
360.nuance: ஈனுலகு and தேனுலகு pair this world and the sweet world above. வேள்வாய்க் கவட்டை is obscure; it is read as the fork where a road parts, both ways being good.

story.act: no story; the proverb's forked road leads well either way

pazhamozhi.applied_to: daily aram serves in both worlds

361.reading: Those who did not readily do the many kinds of good deeds before death, but think of the way later and turn to aram when they see illness, find nothing in it, as a man who sees a dog finds no stone to hand.
361.nuance: ஆய்வின்றி is read as 'without hanging back'; it could also mean 'without discernment'. The proverb says the means is missing at the moment of need, not only that time is short.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way one does not see a stone when one sees a dog

story.act: no story; the proverb's man finds no stone when the dog comes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram put off until illness comes fails

362.reading: When one gets wealth by blameless work and the gathered kinds and the capital are all of that, to be angered when told to do aram generously with it is like spurning milk sweetened with sugar.
362.nuance: Line 1's தக்கமில் and line 2's தொக்க வகையும் முதலும் are hard; the sense rests on the proverb. செருக்கும் is read as refusing in pride.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way one spurns milk with sugar

story.act: no story; the proverb's man spurns sweetened milk

pazhamozhi.applied_to: resenting the call to give from honestly earned wealth refuses one's own good

363.reading: Making those who will not take up good aram take it, checking them with an eye to the lasting good in the endless world, is like mothers who shake the struggling, crying baby that will not feed and pour milk into it.
363.nuance: The verse approves compulsion for the other's good: the unwilling are made to take aram as an infant is fed against its will. குலைத்தடக்கி is read as shaking and holding down. The quotation mark falls after மலைத்தழு(து), so the crying is outside the proverb as printed though it belongs to its image.

pazhamozhi.proverb: உண்ணாக் குழவியைத் தாயார் அலைத்துப்பால் பெய்து விடல்
pazhamozhi.literal: mothers shaking a baby that will not feed and pouring milk into it

story.act: no story; the proverb's mothers force-feed a refusing infant

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unwilling should be made to take aram for their lasting good

364.reading: If even those who do aram look to where it is rightly placed and give with discernment of the ways, it is good for them where they go, their wealth grows as they give it out, and when aram is done, what is not aram departs.
364.nuance: புறஞ்செய்ய is read as giving outward to others. The proverb's அல்லவை, the things that are not good, leave when aram is done.

pazhamozhi.literal: when aram is done, the things that are not good leave
pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram given with discernment brings good hereafter and removes evil

365.reading: Since human birth is hard to come by, the verse urges aram as far as one can, for without fail dreaded disease, old age and hard Death come together, and the stupor comes that puts one to sleep.
365.nuance: The whole of lines 3 and 4 is set as the proverb. துயக்கு and துஞ்ச make death a sleep of bewilderment rather than an event.

pazhamozhi.proverb: அஞ்சும் பிணிமூப்(பு) அருங்கூற்(று) உடனியைந்து துஞ்ச வருமே துயக்கு
pazhamozhi.literal: dreaded disease, old age and hard Death join, and stupor comes to put one to sleep

story.act: no story; the proverb names the three that come together at life's end

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the rare human birth should be used for aram before death

366.reading: If a good aram, planned to be firmly bound so that many are not burdened by how it falls out, meets obstacles and breaks off midway, it would have been better to be one who never planted it.
366.nuance: நட்டறான் is read as 'one who has not planted'; it could also be read as one who plants and does not cut it off, which would make the proverb a call to carry the aram through. Either way the half-done aram is the fault.

pazhamozhi.literal: rather than fall abandoned midway, better to be one who did not plant

story.act: no story; the proverb's planting abandoned midway

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an aram begun must be carried through, or it were better not begun

367.reading: Even if one cannot do aram on many days, the verse tells a woman whose waist seems to wilt under her girdle to do it on some days with the best things, for good aram does what nothing else does.
367.nuance: The proverb is read as 'hear: good aram does what (nothing else) does'; it could also mean that aram's doing is never undone. The counsel trades frequency for the quality of what is given.

pazhamozhi.literal: hear: good aram does what (others) do not

story.act: no story; a general saying addressed to the listener

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram done even on a few days, with the best, is worth doing

368.reading: Birds snatch drying grain in the blink of an eye even while those watching are watching, and for bright wealth won by tending and guarding too, those who eye it are more than those who keep it.
368.nuance: பார்ப்பார் here means those who look out for it, the covetous, set against காப்பார், keepers; it is not the birth-group word. The verse does not name aram: under this heading the lesson is that wealth will not stay kept, so it is better given.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who watch for it outnumber those who guard

story.act: no story; the proverb's birds that take grain from under the watcher's eye

pazhamozhi.applied_to: guarded wealth is still lost to the many who covet it

369.reading: Having seen the two aged parents one cannot do without perish, will anyone still hold wealth to be the true thing? The verse urges aram in a fitting way, for once a thing rolls, no hill stands in the path to stop it.
369.nuance: இருமுது மக்கள் is read as the two aged parents. The proverb is read as life rolling toward death with nothing to check it; ஊர்ந்துருளின் and குன்று வழியடுப்பது leave the image unclear.

pazhamozhi.literal: when it rolls, no hill blocks the way

story.act: no story; the proverb's rolling thing that nothing stops

pazhamozhi.applied_to: death comes unchecked, so wealth should go to aram

370.reading: Those who know fully that grace is what aram rests on know its root; those who plainly leave that root and abandon it keep a conduct that guards nothing, like letting the hare go to eat a crow.
370.nuance: முதல், the root or capital, makes அருள் the source of aram; the proverb ranks the forsaken thing above what is taken, the hare above the crow.

pazhamozhi.literal: letting go the hare and eating the crow

story.act: no story; the proverb's hunter drops the better prey for the worse

pazhamozhi.applied_to: aram without grace gives up the root for a lesser thing

371.reading: Those who have both penance and aram in this life, if they practise them falsely, earn blame not only in this life but in the next: it is a rope with which they bind themselves.
371.nuance: சலமொழுகல், practising with deceit, is the fault; the image turns the means of merit into the means of the deceiver's own bondage.
371.domain_note: those who profess penance or aram

pazhamozhi.literal: the rope with which one binds oneself

story.act: no story; the proverb's self-binding rope

pazhamozhi.applied_to: false penance and aram bind the false one in both worlds

links.note: Kural 226 makes relieving the hunger of the destitute the place to store wealth; Pazhamozhi 358 denies the hoard is a reserve and calls aram done at the fit place the reserve for the time of need.
links.teaches: Both turn the language of saving onto giving, but Pazhamozhi widens the deposit from the hungry poor to any aram placed with discernment, and its proverb names when the store is drawn on, at the time of exhaustion.
links.list_adds: it joins enjoying wealth, giving it on both sides and choosing the fit occasion as one use set against the hoard, where the couplet names a single act.

links.note: Kural 335 urges good deeds before the hiccup stops the tongue; Pazhamozhi 361 shows those who wait until illness to begin aram and find it of no use.
links.teaches: The Kural sets the deadline at the death rattle; Pazhamozhi sets it earlier, at the first sight of illness, and says aram begun then fails because the means is not to hand, as the stone is not when the dog comes.
links.list_adds: its dog-and-stone proverb adds that the late giver lacks the means as well as the time, a cause the couplet's deadline does not give.

links.note: Kural 96 says sweet speech of good things makes அல்லவை wane and aram grow; Pazhamozhi 364's proverb says that when aram is done, அல்லவை leave, provided it is given with discernment of the fit place.
links.teaches: The two share the pair aram and அல்லவை but run the cause differently: in the Kural speech grows aram and wears down evil, in Pazhamozhi aram itself, placed with discernment, drives evil out, so aram is the fruit in one and the agent in the other.
links.list_adds: it sets good hereafter, growth of wealth and the going of evil together as fruits of one well-placed aram, with discernment as their condition, where the couplet names one fruit of speech.

links.note: Both use death, old age and disease as the spur: Naladiyar 92 to share wealth while it is in hand, Pazhamozhi 365 to do aram while one can.
links.teaches: The same triad backs sharing wealth in the Naladiyar and the use of a rare human birth in Pazhamozhi, which ends the triad with death as a stupor that puts one to sleep, so the urgency rests on the rare chance as well as on the threat.
links.list_adds: it puts the rarity of human birth before the triad of disease, old age and Death, joining a reason of opportunity to the quatrain's reason of threat.

links.note: Naladiyar 37 says the gains of human birth should not be spent serving the body; Pazhamozhi 365 says the hard-won human birth should be used for aram as far as one can before disease, age and Death arrive together.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar argues from what human birth is for; Pazhamozhi adds the deadline, so the rare birth has both a purpose and a closing time, and aram is measured by capacity, ஆற்றும் துணையும்.
links.list_adds: it couples the rarity of the birth with the three that end it, which the quatrain, speaking of gains and the body, does not name.

links.note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die midway; Pazhamozhi 366 applies this to aram and says an aram broken off midway is worse than one never begun.
links.teaches: The Kural guards any task against abandonment; Pazhamozhi makes the rule sharper for aram, ranking the half-done gift below not giving at all, and puts the remedy in the planning that keeps many from being burdened.
links.list_adds: it ranks the abandoned aram below never beginning, a ranking the couplet does not make, and ties firmness of plan to sparing others the burden.

links.note: Kural 33 asks for aram without ceasing, as far as one is able; Pazhamozhi 367 allows that one may not manage it on many days and asks for it on some days with the best things.
links.teaches: Where the Kural measures aram by constancy within capacity, Pazhamozhi concedes the lapse and moves the measure to the quality of the gift, so a few days of the best is accepted where the couplet asks for every day.
links.list_adds: it trades frequency for quality, some days with the best things, which the couplet's 'without ceasing' leaves no room for.

links.note: Naladiyar 280 counts guarding wealth among its bitter sufferings; Pazhamozhi 368 says why guarding is vain: those who eye wealth outnumber those who keep it, as birds take grain under the watcher's eye.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar finds custody painful; Pazhamozhi finds it futile, since the covetous are always more than the keepers, and under its heading on aram this futility is the argument for giving wealth rather than keeping it.
links.list_adds: its pairing of grain and wealth makes the watcher's failure an image of all custody, where the quatrain lists custody as one of four pains.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 208 counts guarding earned wealth oneself a duty and handing it to the worthless a folly; Pazhamozhi 368 says that even wealth guarded with care is outnumbered by those who eye it.
links.teaches: Read together the book's two verses on custody limit each other: 208 says keep it yourself, 368 says keeping it never wins, so custody is a duty under the wealth heading that the aram heading turns into a reason to give.

links.note: Kural 249 likens aram done without அருள் to a muddled man's sight of truth; Pazhamozhi 370 calls அருள் the root of aram and its abandonment a loss of the greater for the lesser.
links.teaches: The Kural shows graceless aram as an empty act; Pazhamozhi names grace as aram's root and adds the cost of leaving it, the hare given up for a crow, so the fault is a bad exchange as well as a blindness.
links.list_adds: its hare-and-crow proverb ranks grace above whatever aram is done without it, a ranking of goods the couplet's simile of sight does not give.

links.note: Kural 276 calls those who deceive as if renounced while unrenounced in heart the hardest of all; Pazhamozhi 371 extends false practice to aram as well as penance and says it binds the deceiver in both worlds.
links.teaches: The Kural judges the false renouncer by his cruelty to others; Pazhamozhi turns the harm back on him, a rope he ties on himself, and carries the blame into the next life, so the fraud is self-ruin as much as an injury.
links.list_adds: it pairs penance with aram as the two things that can be falsely kept and this life's blame with the next, which the couplet, speaking only of renunciation, does not.

links.note: Thirikadugam 23 calls giving, faultless conduct and a mind free of possessions a rope that binds good deeds; Pazhamozhi 371 calls penance and aram practised falsely a rope that binds oneself.
links.teaches: The same rope image holds merit fast in Thirikadugam and holds the person fast in Pazhamozhi, so whether giving and penance are a rope that secures good or one that ties up the doer turns on sincerity.

links.note: Naladiyar 342 shows the base man refusing with excuses when urged toward the faultless; Pazhamozhi 363 says those who will not take up aram should be made to take it, as a mother feeds a refusing infant.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar treats refusal of the good as a mark of baseness and leaves it there; Pazhamozhi treats the refuser as a child to be fed by force, so refusal becomes a ground for compulsion rather than contempt.
links.list_adds: its mother-and-infant image adds a remedy and a motive, the other's lasting good, to the quatrain's bare portrait of refusal.

links.note: Both name the road after death with செல்வுழி: Naladiyar 328 mocks the fool who does not tie on its provisions; Pazhamozhi 359 shows the worthy making great wealth a protection for it.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar sets clutching wealth against provision for the road; Pazhamozhi's cane both chewed and boiled into jaggery lets the same wealth serve now and keep for later, so present use and provision are not opposed.
links.list_adds: its cane-and-jaggery proverb holds enjoyment and provision in one use of wealth, where the quatrain sets the grip on wealth against the provision.

source_issues: 360 line 4: the proverb வேள்வாய்க் கவட்டை நெறி is obscure; வேள்வாய் cannot be fixed.
362 lines 1-2: தக்கமில் and தொக்க வகையும் முதலும் are hard to construe; the reading rests on the proverb.
363 line 3: the opening quotation mark falls after மலைத்தழு(து), which has a bracketed ending in our text; the crying belongs to the proverb's image though printed outside it.
364, 366 line 3, 359 line 3: the proverb opens mid-line.
365 line 3: பிணிமூப்(பு) and அருங்கூற்(று) carry bracketed endings, editorial restorations of the syllable.
366 line 4: நட்டறான் can be divided more than one way, giving opposite senses to the proverb.
369 lines 3-4: the proverb ஊர்ந்துருளின் குன்று வழியடுப்ப தில் is unclear.
